description: FlameAtlas turns decades of NASA microgravity fire research into an interactive map showing when any spacecraft material burns or self-extinguishes, with an AI assistant that answers questions using cited NASA evidence and flags where data runs out.
summary: FlameAtlas is a microgravity fire-safety explorer built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 "Flame in Freefall." It predicts whether spacecraft materials will burn in microgravity using a gradient-boosting model trained on NASA PSI and NTRS combustion data from experiments including BASS-II, Saffire, FLEX, CFI, and ACME. Users input oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow velocity, and material type to receive a prediction with probabilities, nearest real experiments, and clickable NASA citations. The tool addresses the critical need for spacecraft fire safety where Earth-based tests fail to predict microgravity behavior, supporting safer Moon and Mars missions.
details:
FlameAtlas is an interactive web dashboard that predicts flame-spread regime in microgravity conditions. Users input oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow velocity, and material type. A gradient-boosting model trained on 620 curated test records from NASA PSI and NTRS predicts whether the material will spread, self-extinguish, or hover near the burn boundary. Each prediction returns probabilities, nearest real NASA experiments with citations, and an out-of-range warning when conditions fall outside tested data.

The system uses NASA PSI experiment tables (PSI-25 BASS-II, PSI-26 BASS, PSI-98 Saffire-I, PSI-99 Saffire-II, PSI-68 FLEX-2, PSI-69 FLEX, PSI-39 CFI, PSI-159 ACME CFI-G, PSI-20 ACME BRE) and NTRS research papers including BASS-II Summary Report (NTRS 20210011385), Saffire IV/V preliminary results (NTRS 20210011521), Saffire operation status (NTRS 20170000230), BASS-II flame spread in exploration atmospheres (NTRS 20080034883), Flammability of Materials on the Moon (NTRS 20240015307), and Nomex flammability for FM2 (NTRS 20250010975). It is built with Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly.js, and deployed on Render. All raw NASA data is publicly available; processed data is committed to GitHub.

The project is creative because it translates decades of scattered NASA combustion research into an interactive tool for spacecraft designers. The team prioritized data honesty: no silent extrapolation, explicit uncertainty flags, and full citation of sources.
